Children and Symbols
How young children relate to symbolic representations such as
pictures and models
A What most distinguishes humans from researchers had a unique opportunity
other creatures is our ability to create
and use a wide range of symbolic
representations, such as pictures and
models. This capacity enables us to
transmit information from one
generation to another, and to learn
without having direct experience —- we
all know about dinosaurs despite
never having met one. Because of the
fundamental role of symbols in almost
everything we do, perhaps no aspect
of human development is more
important than becoming symbol-
minded, and it is fascinating to
examine how young children begin to
use and understand symbolic objects.
The first type of symbolic object
young children master is the picture.
The idea of a picture as a symbol
seems very simple to adults, but
research has discovered that infants
initially find pictures puzzling. It has
been remarked that infants do not
understand the nature of pictures: a
very young child may try to pick up an
apple from a picture, or to fit a foot
into a photograph of a shoe. Judy
DeLoache of the University of Virginia
and three colleagues decided to
investigate such behaviours.
They found out that the behaviours
were far from unusual. When
confronted by a book containing
highly realistic colour photographs of
objects, most nine-month-old infants
reached out to feel or pat the pictures,
sometimes even grasping at them as if
trying to pick them off the page. The
to see how universal this response
was when anthropologist Alma
Gottlieb of the University of Illinois
took some of the pictures to a remote
village in Ivory Coast, Africa. Young
babies, who had almost certainly
never seen a picture before, manually
explored the pictures just as the
American babies had done.
This confusion seems to be conceptual
rather than being based ona
misperception. Infants can easily
distinguish the difference between
objects and pictures. Given a choice
between the two, they choose the real
thing. However, they do not fully
understand what pictures are and
how they differ from the things
depicted, and so they explore. They
only do so, however, when the
depicted object is very similar to the
object it represents. When pictures
bear less resemblance to the real
thing — as in a line drawing — infants
rarely explore them.
Pictures are not the only source of
symbol confusion for very young
children. When a group of toddlers
and their parents were visiting a
laboratory in connection with a
completely unrelated experiment,
researchers were astonished to see
the children try to sit down ina
miniature chair. The researchers then
devised an experiment in which they
brought 18- to 30-month-old children
into a room that contained, among
other things, three large toys: a slide,

a child-sized chair, and a car that
toddlers could sit in and propel
around the room with their feet. When
a child had played with each of the
objects twice, he or she was taken
from the room. The large objects were
then replaced with miniature versions,
only about five inches (12.5cm) tall.
When the child returned, no comment
was made about the switch, and the
child was allowed to play
spontaneously. Almost half of the
children made what the researchers
called ‘scale errors’ by attempting to
perform actions that were impossible
because of extreme differences in the
relative size of the child's body and
the target object. Some tried to sit
down on the little chair, others
attempted to climb the steps of the
slide, causing it to fall over, and a few
tried to get into the miniature car.
The researchers’ interpretation of the
scale errors was that they originated
in a disconnection between the use of
visual information for planning an
action and that for controlling its
execution. When a child saw a
miniature object, visual information
activated their remembered
representation of the object.
Associated with that memory was the
motor programme for interacting with
the large object. Once the child began
to carry out an action, they used visual
information about the actual size of
the object. Some children, for instance,
bent over the very small chair and
looked between their legs to locate it;
those trying to get into the miniature
car first opened its door and then tried
to push their foot in. They relied on
remembered information linking the
replica to the normal-sized object, but
in carrying out their plan, they used
information about the replica’s actual
size to guide their actions.
The concept of dual representation —
the relationship between an object
and its pictorial symbol or replica —
11
has implications for education.
Teachers in pre-school or elementary
school classrooms around the world
use coloured blocks, rods and other
objects designed to represent
numerical quantity. The idea is that
these concrete objects help children to
understand abstract mathematical
principles. But if children do not
understand the relationship between
the objects and what they symbolise,
their use could be counterproductive.
A group of researchers tested the
effects of symbolic objects on
children’s learning about letters and
numbers. Using blocks designed to
teach mathematics, six- and seven-
year-olds were taught to do
subtraction problems. A comparison
group did the problems using pencil
and paper. Both groups learned to
solve the problems equally well, but
the group using the blocks took three
times as long to do so. A child who
used the blocks offered the
researchers some advice: ‘Have you
ever thought of teaching kids to do
these with pencil and paper? It’s a lot
easier!’
